newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ govt tries to please all with debut budget.
newsitem.headline: NZ govt tries to please all with debut budget.

text.p: New Zealand's centre-right coalition government delivered its maiden budget on Thursday, detailing plans for NZ$5.0 billion ($3.43 billion) of spending on social priorities, and projecting continued budget surpluses.
After half a year of political preparation that has been clouded by minor scandals and internal wrangling, the two-party government also unveiled some surprise economic reforms.
Financial markets, often the harshest critics of spending programmes, gave a neutral response to the overall mix of policy and accounts that chart a course for the next three years.
But the government's admission that a current slowdown in growth had undercut the level of its 1997/98 operating surplus was clearly flagged and left bond and share prices unmoved.
Economists welcomed unexpected pledges to speed up the pace of tariff removal, aiming to get rid of all of them well before 2010, and to make state-owned businesses more efficient.
Treasurer Winston Peters, who's upstart New Zealand First party won the balance of power in last October's election, called it a "sound and compassionate budget".
Prime Minister Jim Bolger, leader of the conservative National Party, said the budget would help the country "set and reach goals that only a few years ago were beyond most of us".
Both men were at pains to stress that the budget showed a government with a united political front

"This budget demonstrates we do have a plan, and we do know where we're going, particularly in the areas of social responsibility (and) reduced costs for New Zealand taxpayers," Peters told Reuters Financial Television in an interview.
Political observers have said one of the main challenges facing the two component ruling parties has been how to address the different needs of NZ First and National's power bases.
Raised spending on education and health, tempered with a plan for a benefit delivery system that will put obligations of responsibility on those receiving help, is NZ First ground.
For National, which built its international image in the 1980s and 1990s, policy that shows the continuation of New Zealand's reforming spirit is a priority area.
The compromise served up on Thursday was what Bolger called "responsible and caring spending, tempered by financial imperatives that avoid the pitfalls of debt".
The key figure -- the balance of the state books after the current operating year starting on July 1 -- is for a surplus of NZ$1.5 billion, or half the level forecast in March.
Peters said the Treasury now expected this surplus to be followed by $1.9 billion in 1998/99 and $2.6 billion in 1999/00, backed by a sharp acceleration in GDP growth.
Economic analysts contacted by Reuters said the forecast of a jump in the annual growth rate to 4.2 percent in 1998/99 from a subdued 2.4 percent in 1997/98 was optimistic but reachable.

The recovery scenario is underpinned by hopes of renewed international economic growth, which would kick-start New Zealand's export-driven primary industries, as well as expectations of lower interest rates here and world-wide.

David Plank, an economist at Bankers Trust New Zealand, said: "I think lots of other people in the market will see their growth number for 1998/99 as too high, but it's reasonably close to our pick of 3.9 percent.
"If you were looking at this budget, there would be no reason for you to decide that the risk premium on New Zealand assets should change from what you had it at before."

Business people and financial markets believe Friday's Monetary Policy Statement from the Reserve Bank of New Zealand could do more to change their lot, as it could herald lower interest rates and possible a weaker New Zealand dollar.
